---
title: "Can weight and horsepower explain fuel economy?"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Can weight and horsepower explain fuel economy?}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

Can we describe fuel economy using a car's weight and horsepower? We will fit
one model, read its coefficients and inspect what it misses. In these data,
heavier cars and cars with more horsepower tend to have lower fuel economy,
after accounting for the other predictor. The model describes about 83% of the
observed variation, but several cars still have sizable residuals.

## Understand the data

**Example data: R's built-in mtcars dataset**

The data contain 32 cars from a motor magazine's road tests. Fuel economy
(`mpg`) is measured in miles per US gallon, weight (`wt`) in thousands of pounds
and engine power (`hp`) in gross horsepower. Each row is a car; the row names
retain its model name. These are observational measurements, so associations
between the variables do not establish what a weight or engine change would
cause for a particular car.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center")
```

```{r data, message=FALSE}
library(olsrr)
car_data <- datasets::mtcars[c("mpg", "wt", "hp")]
stopifnot(nrow(car_data) == 32L, !anyNA(car_data))
head(car_data)
```

We check the three columns we will actually use. None is missing, so every
calculation below refers to the same 32 cars. When adapting this example,
decide how to handle missing measurements before comparing results: a change
in the rows can also change the apparent fit.

## Fit once and read the result

Use R's `lm()` to specify the response on the left of `~` and the two predictors
on the right. Adding `wt` and `hp` gives each predictor its own straight-line
contribution; this formula does not include an interaction. The fitted object
keeps the model and observations together for the following steps.

```{r regression}
fuel_model <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = car_data)
ols_regress(fuel_model)
```

Read the **Beta** column in the response's units. Holding horsepower fixed,
an additional 1,000 pounds is associated with about 3.88 fewer miles per
gallon. Holding weight fixed, an additional horsepower is associated with
about 0.032 fewer miles per gallon, or 0.32 fewer for ten horsepower.
These are comparisons within the fitted model, rather than two separate
regressions or instructions for modifying a vehicle.

The **lower** and **upper** columns give 95% confidence intervals under the
usual model assumptions. For weight the interval is about -5.17 to -2.58 mpg
per 1,000 pounds. It expresses uncertainty about the conditional slope;
it is not a range containing 95% of cars. The intercept describes a car with
zero weight and zero horsepower, outside this sample's useful range.

## Inspect what remains unexplained

A residual is observed fuel economy minus the model's fitted fuel economy.
A positive residual means the car used less fuel per mile than the model
suggested, because its observed mpg was higher. Plotting residuals against
fitted values helps reveal patterns hidden by the regression table.

```{r residual-plot, fig.cap="Fuel-economy residuals for the 32 mtcars observations, in miles per US gallon.", fig.alt="Residual fuel economy against fitted mpg for 32 cars. Several residuals exceed five mpg, and the highest fitted values include large positive residuals above the zero line."}
residual_plot <- ols_plot_resid_fit(fuel_model, print_plot = FALSE)
residual_plot
```

Several residuals are above five mpg, and the high fitted values include
large positive residuals. This is reason to investigate the shape of the
relationship and the individual cars. A high R-squared alone does not show
that the straight-line mean or the uncertainty calculations are adequate.
The plot also does not establish independence between observations.
Here `print_plot = FALSE` returns a ggplot directly, which we then print;
other plotting functions can return lists, so check their individual help.

## Put the fit in perspective

```{r performance}
performance <- ols_model_performance(fuel_model)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Measure = c("R-squared", "Adjusted R-squared", "Predicted R-squared", "RMSE (mpg)"),
  Value = c(performance$rsq, performance$adjr, performance$prsq, performance$rmse)
), digits = 3, caption = "A compact performance summary for the same fuel-economy model.")
```

R-squared is 0.827: the fit accounts for about 83% of the sample variation
in mpg around its mean. The residual RMSE is 2.593 mpg, a measure of the
remaining scatter using the residual degrees of freedom. It is not a
guaranteed error bound for an individual prediction. Predicted R-squared,
0.781, uses leave-one-out prediction errors; it gives a less optimistic
view than training R-squared, but is not independent validation on new cars.

Next, learn to [read a regression table](regression-output.html), then
work through [residual diagnostics](residual-diagnostics.html) to investigate
shape and spread. The function help for
[`ols_regress()`](https://olsrr.rsquaredacademy.com/reference/ols_regress.html),
[`ols_plot_resid_fit()`](https://olsrr.rsquaredacademy.com/reference/ols_plot_resid_fit.html) and
[`ols_model_performance()`](https://olsrr.rsquaredacademy.com/reference/ols_model_performance.html) describes their output
and options. Start with that residual investigation before using this model
to make decisions about cars outside the observed sample.
